concepts.def: UK national standards body founded in 1901 that publishes the BS series of standards.
BSI certification mark indicating a product has been independently tested to meet a relevant British Standard.
British Standard governing technical product documentation, defining how engineering drawings should be prepared.
European conformity mark showing a product meets relevant EU health, safety and environmental requirements.
UK Conformity Assessed marking introduced in 2021 for goods placed on the Great Britain market after Brexit.
Standard published by the International Organization for Standardization, enabling consistency across global markets.

walkthroughs.body_html:
National & International Standards — a core area of A-Level Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

National & International Standards brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with National & International Standards.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Which standard governs UK engineering drawing practice?
options: ISO 9001

mcqs.q: What is the difference between CAD and CAM?
options: They are the same thing with different names.
CAD creates digital designs; CAM uses those designs to control manufacturing machines.
A drawing in black ink only.
CAD is for cars, CAM is for cameras.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between ductility and malleability?
options: Ductility is being drawn into wires; malleability is being hammered into sheets.
Ductility is for metals, malleability is for plastics.
A drawing in black ink only.
They mean exactly the same thing.
A drawing in black ink only.
A drawing showing multiple 2D views (front, side, plan) of an object.
Ductility is for metals, malleability is for plastics.
A 3D drawing showing the object at an angle.
